metaDescription: Six gas log splitters from 18 to 35 tons compared on tonnage, engine size, cycle time and towing so you match the machine to your firewood.
expertTake: The Full Boar 28 ton is the best overall pick because it balances tonnage with a fast 10.9 second cycle in a size most owners can handle. The SuperHandy 20 ton is the value pick for straight seasoned wood. Anyone burning under a cord a year should skip gas and rent a splitter or buy a smaller electric one.
introParagraphs: A gas log splitter is a hydraulic ram driven by a small engine. The engine turns a pump, the pump pushes a cylinder, and the cylinder shoves a round of wood into a steel wedge. Tonnage describes the force, but cycle time and log handling decide how much firewood you actually produce in an afternoon.

The market is crowded with near-identical machines with different stickers, so the differences that matter are pump design, engine size, beam layout and how the machine moves around a yard. This guide decodes those and ranks six splitters by who they suit.

products.name: Full Boar 28 Ton Gas Log Splitter 212cc 49-State
products.description:
The Full Boar 28 ton couples a 212cc OHV engine to a hydraulic system that cycles in about 10.9 seconds, which is quick for a machine in this force class. An auto-return control valve with an adjustable detent saves effort because the ram retracts without you holding the lever. A 28 ton rating is enough for knotty hardwood rounds that stall smaller machines.

The tradeoff is that a 212cc engine is a modest motor for 28 tons, so heavy loads are slowed by the pump rather than the engine. Compared with the 35 ton BILT HARD, it gives up raw force but is lighter, easier to tow around a yard and cheaper to keep fueled. Against the SuperHandy 25 ton it adds three tons and a faster stated cycle.

Ownership is standard small-engine and hydraulic upkeep: check hydraulic fluid before the season, change engine oil, keep the wedge clean and grease the moving parts. Let the machine warm up in cold weather because thick fluid slows the ram.
products.bestFor: Homeowners processing several cords a year of mixed hardwood.
cons: 212cc engine is modest for the tonnage
Cycle time still slower than a kinetic splitter

products.name: BILT HARD 22 Ton Gas Log Splitter 209cc 2-Stage 14 GPM
products.description:
This BILT HARD uses a 14 GPM two-stage gear pump to cut cycle time to about 7 seconds, the fastest in the lineup. A two-stage pump moves fast at low load and shifts to high force when the wedge meets resistance, so the ram does not crawl through easy wood. A 21 inch log capacity covers standard firewood lengths.

The tradeoff is force. At 22 tons it is below the Full Boar 28 ton, and knotty elm or sweetgum rounds can stall it where the bigger machine would push through. For straight seasoned oak and maple it is a speed machine.

Check the hydraulic fluid level before each season, keep the wedge clean and let the engine and fluid warm up in cold weather. A shorter cycle also means more cycles per hour, so watch for heat in a long session.
products.bestFor: Owners who split large volumes of straight, seasoned wood and want speed.
pros: 7 second cycle is the fastest here
cons: Less force than the 28 ton machines
Faster cycling heats fluid in long sessions

products.name: SuperHandy 25 Ton Portable Gas Log Splitter 7HP Bucher
products.description:
SuperHandy's 25 ton model uses a 7HP engine and a two-stage Bucher gear pump, a brand name known in hydraulics, on a half-beam frame designed to be light enough to roll around a yard. The horizontal and vertical layout lets you split on the ground for long rounds or stand logs for heavy lifting.

The tradeoff is beam length and cycle speed. A half-beam is lighter than a full beam but may have a shorter stroke, and a 7HP engine is the minimum for the tonnage. Compared with the Full Boar 28 ton it is lighter and easier to manage but offers three tons less.

Ownership is routine: fluid check, oil change, wedge cleaning and a quick grease. Keep the breather vented while running and plugged for transport as the manual says.
products.bestFor: Owners who want 25 tons in a machine they can move by hand.
cons: Half beam may limit log length
7HP is a minimum engine for this force
Slower than the 22 ton BILT HARD

products.name: BILT HARD 35 Ton Horizontal Vertical Gas Log Splitter 301cc
products.description:
The BILT HARD 35 ton puts a 301cc 10HP engine behind the highest force in the group. Sixteen inch DOT-certified tires and a full beam frame mean it is built to be towed and to handle large, heavy rounds that smaller machines refuse. It splits horizontally or vertically.

The tradeoff is the machine itself. A 35 ton splitter is heavy and slow to move by hand, and the pump usually cycles slower than lighter units. Against the Full Boar 28 ton, it adds seven tons of force for a significant increase in weight and fuel use.

Expect more engine and hydraulic upkeep, and plan for a tow vehicle or ATV. Check the DOT tires and hitch before every trip and keep the beam and wedge cleaned of sap.
products.bestFor: Landowners splitting large green or knotty rounds.
cons: Heavy and hard to move by hand

products.name: SuperHandy 20 Ton Portable Gas Log Splitter 7HP Auto Return
products.description:
The SuperHandy 20 ton is a horizontal full-beam splitter with a 7HP engine, a Bucher gear pump and a rapid auto return ram system. Twenty tons is the entry point for gas splitting and handles most straight seasoned logs. The full beam design is sturdy for its weight.

The tradeoff is that 20 tons is the minimum for hardwoods with knots, so heavy, green rounds will stall it. Compared with the SuperHandy 25 ton, it is lighter but less forceful, and compared with the 18 ton BILT HARD it is slightly stronger.

Upkeep is the usual fluid, oil and wedge checks. Run it on level ground with the wheels chocked and keep hands clear of the wedge. Because it is the most affordable way into hydraulic splitting here, owners tend to push it beyond its comfort zone, so cut oversized rounds down with a chainsaw first and the pump will thank you for it over many seasons.
products.bestFor: Firewood burners who split straight, seasoned logs.
pros: 20 ton force at a modest size

products.name: BILT HARD 18 Ton 7HP 209cc Portable Gas Log Splitter
products.description:
The BILT HARD 18 ton is the smallest gas splitter in the group, with a 209cc 7HP engine, a steel wedge and a fast auto return. It is portable and easy to store, which makes it a sensible machine for a couple of cords a year.

The tradeoff is force. Eighteen tons splits softwoods and straight seasoned hardwood, but gnarled rounds will stop it cold. Against the 22 ton BILT HARD it saves weight but loses speed and force.

Keep fluid topped up, change the oil and keep the wedge clean. A small machine is easy to overwork, so cut very large rounds with a saw first.
products.bestFor: Light firewood use where gas power is wanted at a small size.
cons: Short on reserve for green hardwood

buyingCriteria.explanation: Tonnage is pump pressure times cylinder area, and the number matters most when the wood is knotty or green. Straight seasoned oak and maple split fine at 18 to 22 tons, while knotty elm or sweetgum calls for 25 tons or more. The BILT HARD 18 and SuperHandy 20 fit the first group, the Full Boar 28 and BILT HARD 35 the second. A common mistake is buying 35 tons to split wood that a 22 ton would handle, which adds weight, fuel burn and a slower stroke for no benefit. The opposite mistake is just as costly: a machine that stalls on every third round turns a pleasant afternoon into a stop-start chore.

Cycle time is the time for the ram to go out and return, and it sets how many logs you split per hour. The BILT HARD 22 claims 7 seconds, the Full Boar 28 about 10.9 seconds, and heavier machines are slower. Faster is better until the pump loses force, so compare cycle time with tonnage and not alone. Remember too that the cycle is only part of the job: loading the round, positioning it and tossing split pieces aside usually takes longer than the stroke itself, so a log lift or a comfortable working height can save more time than shaving a second off the ram.

Single-stage pumps hold full force but move slowly, while two-stage pumps run fast at low load and shift to high force when the wedge meets resistance. The BILT HARD 22 lists a 14 GPM two-stage pump and the SuperHandy models use Bucher two-stage gear pumps. A two-stage pump is the single most useful hydraulic feature for productivity. Single-stage designs are not wrong, but they commit you to a slow stroke on every log, easy or hard, so a seasoned-wood burner who splits several cords a year will feel the difference within the first afternoon.

The engine turns the pump, so displacement sets how much load the pump can take before the engine bogs. A 301cc 10HP engine in the BILT HARD 35 carries the pump easily, while a 212cc engine in the Full Boar 28 is working harder. Look for OHV engines and an easily accessible choke and oil check. Also confirm that the engine has a low-oil shutoff, since a splitter pump that is run hard on a hot afternoon with a low crankcase is the quickest way to turn a good machine into a repair bill.

A horizontal splitter lets you roll rounds on the beam, and a vertical mode lets you stand heavy logs on end and split without lifting. The Full Boar and BILT HARD models offer both. Log lift accessories save your back on heavy rounds. Check maximum log length as well, since a 21 inch capacity is typical.

A 35 ton machine with DOT tires such as the BILT HARD 35 is built to be towed, while lighter units are pulled by hand. Check tire pressure, hitch rating and local rules for highway towing. If you only split at home, a lighter unit that you can push by hand is more convenient than a heavy towable.

specDecoder.watchFor: The BILT HARD 22 lists 7 seconds and the Full Boar 28 about 10.9.

specDecoder.meaning: A pump that moves fast under light load and switches to high force under heavy load.
specDecoder.watchFor: Both SuperHandy models name a Bucher pump and the BILT HARD 22 names a 14 GPM two-stage pump.

howWeEvaluated.title: Splitting force
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated tonnage with the pump and engine behind it. A machine that promised more force than its engine could drive was marked down. The 18 to 35 ton range in this lineup shaped the ranking.

howWeEvaluated.title: Speed
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared cycle times and pump type. The BILT HARD 22 at 7 seconds and the Full Boar 28 at about 10.9 seconds set the range. Claimed times are treated as claims.

howWeEvaluated.title: Handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at beam layout, wheels, tires and log lift options. Machines with both horizontal and vertical modes scored higher. Heavy machines lost points for moving by hand.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered fluid care, engine upkeep and parts access from listings and owner feedback patterns. Simpler machines scored better on upkeep. Brand history was a minor factor.

howWeEvaluated.title: Match to use
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched each machine to a likely firewood volume and wood type. The 18 ton BILT HARD suits a couple of cords while the 35 ton suits heavy rounds. Scores reflect the spec sheet.

rows: Mixed hardwood on a light frame

cards.label: Fast cycle
cards.text: The BILT HARD 22 at 7 seconds moves through straight wood quickly and saves time on large volumes. It is the best choice if your wood is seasoned and clean.

cards.label: High tonnage
cards.text: The Full Boar 28 and BILT HARD 35 push through knots and green wood at the cost of speed and weight. They are the best choice if your wood is difficult.

howToChoose.note: Pick fast cycle for easy wood and high tonnage for hard wood.

rows: Push by hand around the yard

howToChoose.subheading: For Large Annual Firewood Needs Specifically

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Look for a two-stage pump, a cycle time near or below 11 seconds, a vertical mode for heavy rounds and a log lift for large pieces. A bigger engine keeps the pump supplied through a long session.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Full Boar 28 Ton and BILT HARD 22 Ton are the best match for several cords a year. The 35 ton model adds force for heavy rounds at a cost in weight.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Spend more if your wood is green, knotty or oversized. The Full Boar 28 Ton and BILT HARD 35 Ton earn their cost by not stalling on tough rounds.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Save if you split a couple of cords of seasoned wood. The SuperHandy 20 Ton or BILT HARD 18 Ton is enough.

maintenance.why: Low fluid starves the pump and makes the ram jerky. Use the oil the manual specifies.
Small engines run hot under load. Fresh oil protects the engine.
Sap and rounded edges slow splitting. A clean wedge cuts with less force.
Dry slide surfaces and bearings wear quickly. Grease keeps movement smooth.
Old fuel gums the carburetor and causes hard starts.

faq.q: How many tons do I need?
faq.a: For straight seasoned wood, 18 to 22 tons is enough. For knotty or green hardwood, 25 to 28 tons is a safer range. Thirty-five tons is for heavy rounds and landowners.
Yes, it sets how many logs you split per hour. A 7 second cycle is nearly twice as fast as a 12 second cycle. Compare it against tonnage.
Horizontal is easier for smaller rounds. Vertical lets you stand heavy rounds and split without lifting. Machines with both modes are the most flexible.

faq.q: How do I keep it running in cold weather?
faq.a: Let the engine and fluid warm up before heavy use. Thick fluid slows the pump and causes jerky motion. Use the fluid grade the manual specifies.
Yes, but green wood is stringy and needs more force. Seasoned wood splits cleaner. A 4-way wedge halves the number of passes on straight rounds.
Only with proper habits. Keep hands off the wedge path, use the control lever as designed and wear eye and foot protection. Shut off the engine before adjusting anything.
